Arkansas statutes set the basic rules between landlords and tenants, including deposits, notices and what happens when a rental is sold.

What the official sources say

  • Security deposit may not exceed two months' rent; the AG notes the security-deposit law applies only to landlords who rent six or more units. (Arkansas Attorney General, Landlord And Tenant Rights (security deposits); source)
  • Landlord must return the deposit within 60 days after the tenant moves out and, if deducting, provide a written itemized list of charges within 60 days of vacating; entire deposit may be withheld if damages or unpaid rent exceed it. (Arkansas Attorney General, Landlord And Tenant Rights; source)
  • Landlord must give notice of at least one rental period before raising rent, for oral and written leases. (Arkansas Attorney General, Landlord And Tenant Rights; source)
  • A landlord may give notice of lease termination for any reason: one rental period's notice for an oral lease, or notice per the terms of a written lease. (Arkansas Attorney General, Landlord And Tenant Rights; source)
  • AG states Arkansas laws on these issues apply only to private rental units, not government-subsidized housing. (Arkansas Attorney General, Landlord And Tenant Rights; source)

Which Arkansas laws cover landlords and tenants?

The main statute is the Arkansas Residential Landlord-Tenant Act of 2007, found in Chapter 17 of Title 18 of the Arkansas Code. The Attorney General adds that these rules apply to private rental units and not to government-subsidized housing.

Legal Aid of Arkansas describes the Act as a law meant to simplify and modernize residential rental rules. It sets out what a rental agreement may contain, such as rent and the length of the term, and the steps to follow when either side breaks the agreement. Some living arrangements fall outside it. Section 18-17-202 lists them, and Legal Aid names institutional residences for medical, educational or religious services, stays in hotels and motels that are subject to sales tax, and protective shelters.

The Act also puts duties on the renter. Section 18-17-601 requires a tenant to follow housing codes that affect health and safety, keep the unit clean and safe, dispose of waste in a reasonable way and keep plumbing fixtures reasonably clean. The Attorney General notes that both oral and written leases bind the parties, though a written lease avoids arguments about who promised what.

How do Arkansas security deposit rules work?

Arkansas caps a deposit at two months' rent, but only for landlords who rent six or more dwellings. The table shows the main points from the Attorney General and Legal Aid of Arkansas.

QuestionAnswerSource
Who is covered?Landlords who rent six or more dwellings; Legal Aid also counts a landlord who has someone manage or collect rentAttorney General; Legal Aid
Maximum depositTwo months' rentAttorney General
Deadline to return it60 days after the tenant moves outAttorney General
If money is keptA written, itemized list of charges within 60 days of vacatingAttorney General
Can the landlord keep it all?Yes, when damage or unpaid rent exceeds the depositAttorney General
If the landlord ignores the rulesThe tenant may be owed twice the deposit plus costs and attorney's feesLegal Aid

A landlord with five or fewer properties falls outside these provisions, Legal Aid says. In that case the written lease matters even more, and a tenant can still sue in small claims court for the deposit, where the landlord may counterclaim for unpaid rent or damage. Legal Aid also says that if a landlord cannot find the former tenant after a reasonable attempt, the landlord may keep the whole deposit after 180 days.

What notice does a landlord owe for rent increases and lease endings?

A landlord must give notice of at least one rental period before raising the rent, on oral and written leases alike. The Attorney General also says a landlord may end a lease for any reason, with one rental period's notice on an oral lease or the notice the written lease calls for.

  • A tenant who wants to sublease usually needs the landlord's approval first, plus written direction on how much rent can be collected.
  • A tenant leaving a written lease follows the lease's notice terms, and a tenant leaving an oral lease gives one rental period's notice.
  • Under the Act, a week-to-week tenancy ends on seven days' written notice and a month-to-month tenancy on 30 days' written notice, from either side (§ 18-17-704).

Legal Aid adds that a landlord who declines to renew may do so for any reason except those the Fair Housing Act forbids.

Who has to make repairs in an Arkansas rental?

It depends on when the lease was signed. The Attorney General's guidance says renters usually take a house or apartment as is, and a landlord is not required to provide extra maintenance beyond what city building codes demand. Any promised repair should be written into the lease. A tenant should keep paying rent even if a promised repair is not done, and the Attorney General points to small claims court, renegotiating, moving out or a private attorney as recourse.

A 2021 law changed the picture for newer leases. Under § 18-17-502, leases signed or renewed after November 1, 2021 carry implied standards for a dwelling or single-family house: running hot and cold water, electricity, drinking water, a sanitary sewer and plumbing that meet code, a functioning roof and building envelope, and heating and air conditioning if the home had them at lease signing.

The statute has some safe harbors for landlords. A landlord is treated as compliant if the tenant is handed a written defect form at move-in and either signs it without listing a defect or fails to return it within two business days. Defects caused by the tenant, the tenant's family or visitors do not count against the landlord. A tenant can install a battery-powered or plug-in smoke or carbon monoxide detector at personal expense, and then becomes responsible for keeping it working. A city or county with stricter housing standards still applies its own rules.

What can a landlord do when a tenant breaks the lease?

The landlord's first tool is written notice. Section 18-17-701 allows a notice that names the acts or omissions and says the agreement will end at least 14 days after receipt unless the problem is fixed. Unpaid rent works faster: if rent is not paid within five days of the due date, the landlord may terminate.

A tenant who refuses lawful access can be ordered by a district court to allow it, since § 18-17-705 lets the landlord seek an injunction. A landlord may recover actual damages and, when represented by a lawyer, attorney's fees if nonpayment was not in good faith. The full eviction steps, from the three-day unlawful detainer notice to the sheriff's writ, are laid out on our Arkansas eviction process page.

What does the Fair Housing Act add?

It bars discrimination in renting or selling a dwelling based on race, color, religion, gender, handicap, familial status or national origin. The Attorney General lists several specific bans.

  • Advertisements that signal a preference or limit, such as adults-only for part of a complex.
  • Different terms or conditions of sale or rent.
  • Discrimination in the use of facilities tied to the dwelling.
  • Assigning a person to a particular section of a complex or a particular floor.

Complaints can go to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development or the Arkansas Fair Housing Commission.

How does selling a rental house change these rules?

Selling does not end the duties above on its own. The statutes cited here speak to the landlord and the tenant, and none of them says a sale cancels a lease, so the lease terms and an attorney's advice should come first.

Owners considering a sale usually weigh a few facts. A month-to-month tenant can be given 30 days' written notice, and a landlord who will not renew needs a lawful reason, which in Arkansas can be any reason that is not discriminatory. The deposit is a separate matter: ask the closing attorney how the deposit and any prepaid rent will be handled so the tenant's refund rights are not left hanging.

A rented house also changes tax paperwork. The Assessment Coordination Division asks owners to notify the assessor when a house goes from owner-occupied to rental, and the transfer tax of $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration applies to the deed. In Little Rock, privately owned rentals with two or more dwellings must meet the city's minimum housing standards, which include working plumbing, electricity and a roof that does not leak.

Where can landlords and tenants get help in Arkansas?

Legal Aid of Arkansas runs a landlord and tenant guide and a free helpline at 1-800-952-9243 for people who qualify. The Attorney General's page also points to the Arkansas Community Action Agencies. In Little Rock, the Department of Housing and Neighborhood Programs takes housing code complaints at (501) 371-6825, and residents can call 211 for utility and housing help.

More questions about Arkansas Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

What is the maximum security deposit in Arkansas?

Two months' rent. The cap applies to landlords who rent six or more dwellings, so a landlord with fewer properties is not bound by that statute, though the lease still controls.

How long does a landlord have to return a deposit in Arkansas?

Sixty days after the tenant moves out. A landlord who deducts must send a written, itemized list of charges within the same 60 days, according to the Attorney General.

Can an Arkansas landlord raise the rent whenever they want?

No. The landlord must give notice of at least one rental period before raising rent, whether the lease is oral or written. Check the lease for any terms about rent during a fixed term.

Does a tenant have to keep paying rent if the landlord skips a repair?

Yes. Section 18-17-502 says a tenant may not withhold or offset rent over implied quality standards. After written notice and 30 calendar days with rent current, the tenant's sole remedy is to end the lease without penalty and recover a deposit that is owed.

Do these laws cover subsidized housing?

No. The Attorney General states that Arkansas landlord and tenant laws apply only to private rental units, not government-subsidized housing.

Can a landlord end a lease so the owner can sell?

The Attorney General says a landlord may end a lease for any reason with the required notice. The sources do not list a sale as a special ground, so a lawyer should confirm the notice period for your lease before you send it.

Arkansas law requires a landlord to give a specific written notice before filing an eviction, and the number of days depends on the reason.

What the official sources say

  • Nonpayment of rent: landlord must give three days' written notice to vacate; if tenant does not leave, landlord sues by complaint in court (unlawful detainer). (Arkansas Attorney General, Landlord And Tenant Rights; source)
  • After service of summons, tenant has five days to object in writing filed with the court clerk; if no objection, the county sheriff can remove the tenant; if objection, a hearing is scheduled. (Arkansas Attorney General, Landlord And Tenant Rights; source)
  • No-cause termination: one rental period's notice for an oral lease, or as the written lease provides. (Arkansas Attorney General, Landlord And Tenant Rights; source)
Selling in Arkansas?
We buy Arkansas houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What written notice does an Arkansas landlord give before filing an eviction?

It depends on the reason. For unpaid rent, the Arkansas Attorney General describes a three-day written notice to vacate, while the statute treats rent that stays unpaid five days past its due date as legal notice that the landlord may start eviction.

Other problems follow a different clock. If a tenant breaks the lease in some way other than paying late, Ark. Code 18-17-701 lets the landlord deliver a written notice that names the acts or omissions and warns that the rental agreement will end no sooner than 14 days after receipt. A tenant who fixes the problem inside that window keeps the lease, as long as the problem can be fixed.

Arkansas also has an older criminal statute for rent defaults. Under Ark. Code 18-16-101, a tenant who willfully refuses to leave after ten days' written notice commits a misdemeanor, with a fine of $1 to $25 for each day. Most landlords never use it, but owners reading old forms will see the ten-day figure and wonder why it differs from the three-day notice.

SituationNotice or triggerWhere it comes from
Rent unpaidThree days' written notice to vacate (Attorney General summary); five days past due date gives the right to begin evictionAttorney General page; Ark. Code 18-17-901(b)
Other lease breachWritten notice, termination no sooner than 14 days after receipt if not curedArk. Code 18-17-701(a)
Week-to-week tenancyWritten notice at least 7 days before the end dateArk. Code 18-17-704(a)
Month-to-month tenancyWritten notice at least 30 days before the end dateArk. Code 18-17-704(b)
Rent default, criminal trackTen days' written notice, then a misdemeanor if the tenant willfully staysArk. Code 18-16-101

How does an eviction case move once the notice period ends?

The landlord files in district court. Under Ark. Code 18-17-902, the filing is a complaint plus an affidavit of eviction signed by someone with personal knowledge of the grounds. The court then issues an order telling the tenant to leave or show cause why not within ten calendar days of service.

The Attorney General's tenant guide gives a slightly different picture of the tenant's side. It says that after the summons arrives the tenant has five days to object in writing to the court clerk, and that without an objection the county sheriff can remove the tenant. The two descriptions come from different sources and different procedures, so a landlord planning a sale date should confirm the exact deadline with the district court clerk handling the case.

If the tenant shows up and contests, section 18-17-905 says the court hears it like any other civil case. Either side may appeal, and section 18-17-909 sends the appeal through the normal civil route. An appeal is the step that most often stretches a timeline past what an owner expected.

  • Step one: written notice that matches the reason for the eviction.
  • Step two: complaint and affidavit filed in district court.
  • Step three: order to vacate or show cause, served on the tenant.
  • Step four: hearing if the tenant contests, or sheriff removal if no one objects.
  • Step five: possible appeal by either party.

Can an Arkansas landlord end a lease just because they want to sell?

Yes, in most month-to-month and oral arrangements. The Attorney General states that a landlord may give notice of lease termination for any reason, one rental period's notice for an oral lease, or as the written lease provides.

That matters to anyone who has decided to sell a rental house. A fixed-term written lease still controls until it ends, so the owner reads the term and any renewal language first. A month-to-month tenant, by contrast, can be given a written notice of at least 30 days under section 18-17-704. Landlords who need to sell on a short timeline sometimes pick a termination date that lines up with a target closing.

Keep the paper trail clean. Dates on the notice, proof of delivery and a copy of the lease all become evidence if the tenant stays and the case goes to court.

What happens if the tenant stays after the lease ends?

The landlord may bring an action for possession. Section 18-17-704(c) covers holdovers: if the tenant remains without consent after the term ends or the agreement is terminated, the landlord can sue, and attorney's fees are available when the holdover is not in good faith.

A willful holdover carries a heavier remedy. The statute allows recovery of an amount up to three months of periodic rent, or twice the actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees. The landlord also needs to avoid accepting rent in a way that looks like consent to continued occupancy, since section 18-17-704(c)(4) points back to the rule for tenants who stay with the landlord's agreement.

Where the court rules for the tenant, section 18-17-908 says the tenant keeps possession until the tenancy ends by agreement or law, until rent goes unpaid, or until another eviction succeeds. That is one reason a sale contract with a tenant in the house should leave room for delay.

What happens to belongings and the deposit when a tenant leaves?

Arkansas treats property left in the dwelling after a lease ends as abandoned. The Attorney General says the landlord may dispose of it as the landlord sees fit, without recourse by the tenant, and that the property is subject to a lien for sums the tenant agreed to pay.

Deposits have their own rules, but only for larger landlords. The state's security-deposit law applies to those who rent six or more dwellings. For them, the deposit cannot exceed two months' rent, it must be returned within 60 days of move-out, and any deduction needs an itemized written list inside the same 60 days. An owner with one or two rental houses is outside that statute, though the lease may still set its own terms.

  • Photograph the empty house and any left items before touching them.
  • Keep receipts for repairs charged against a deposit.
  • Send the itemized list to the forwarding address within the 60 days where the law applies.
  • Do not change locks or shut off utilities to push a tenant out. Use the court process.

What does an eviction cost in time and money?

The filing fee is set by Ark. Code 16-17-705, as cross-referenced in section 18-17-902, and the district court clerk can quote the current amount. Time is the larger cost. Notice days, service on the tenant, a hearing date and any appeal all add up, and each rental month lost during that period is income the owner does not get back.

Attorney's fees are recoverable in some cases. Section 18-17-701 allows them for willful noncompliance other than nonpayment, and for nonpayment not made in good faith, only when the landlord is represented by an attorney.

Add to that the cost of repairs after move-out. Rental houses that have been through an eviction often need paint, flooring or cleanout work before they can be listed with a traditional agent.

How does a pending eviction affect selling the house?

It narrows the choices. A conventional buyer financed by a lender usually wants possession, an inspection and a repaired house, none of which is easy while a tenant is contesting. Some owners wait out the court process and then list. Others sell the property with the tenant or the open case attached, to a buyer who is willing to take on that risk.

A cash buyer purchases as-is and does not depend on lender repair requirements, which can matter when the house has damage from a difficult tenancy. Whether a sale makes sense before the eviction ends depends on the lease, the notice already served, and the state of the court file. An owner who wants to understand those facts can speak with an Arkansas attorney or the district court clerk before signing a contract.

The Attorney General also reminds owners that the Fair Housing Act applies to the sale and rental of homes. Advertising or terms that show a preference based on race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin are barred, whether the house is rented or sold.

More questions about Arkansas Eviction Notice Rules

What is the notice period for nonpayment of rent in Arkansas?

Three days' written notice to vacate is the figure the Arkansas Attorney General gives for nonpayment. Separately, Ark. Code 18-17-901(b) treats rent unpaid five days after the due date as legal notice that the landlord may begin eviction proceedings.

How long is the notice for a month-to-month tenant in Arkansas?

A landlord or tenant ends a month-to-month tenancy with written notice at least 30 days before the termination date under Ark. Code 18-17-704(b). A week-to-week tenancy needs at least seven days.

Can an Arkansas tenant be arrested for not leaving after notice?

Possibly. Ark. Code 18-16-101 makes it a misdemeanor to willfully refuse to leave after ten days' written notice for failure to pay rent, with a fine of $1 to $25 per day. Landlords more often use the civil eviction route.

Who removes a tenant after an eviction order in Arkansas?

The county sheriff. The Attorney General's guide says a tenant who does not file a written objection can be removed by the sheriff, and the summons in a rent case is directed to the sheriff of the county where the complaint is filed.

Does an Arkansas landlord need a lawyer to evict?

The statutes allow the landlord or the landlord's agent to file the complaint and affidavit. A lawyer is required only to collect attorney's fees, which section 18-17-701 allows when the landlord is represented by an attorney.

What if I want to sell the house while the tenant is still there?

You can discuss a sale, but the tenant keeps rights until the lease ends or a court orders them out. Check the lease term, the notices served and the court file, then speak with an attorney before agreeing to a closing date.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

When property tax goes unpaid in Arkansas, the statutes allow the taxing authority to sell a lien or the property itself, and they give the owner a set time to redeem.

What the official sources say

  • Sale date must be no earlier than one year after the tax-delinquent parcel is certified to the Commissioner of State Lands. (26 CAR 400-104; source)
  • Until the parcel is sold or disposed of by the state, a person may redeem by petition to the Commissioner plus payment of outstanding taxes, penalties, interest, fees and costs; effective July 1, 2023 petitions and payment must be received before 4:00 p.m. CT on the last business day before the auction; partial payments do not extend redemption. (26 CAR 400-108; source)
  • Money from a tax-delinquent sale above taxes, fees, penalties, interest and costs is excess proceeds, distributed on application per statute (Ark. Code 26-37-205); any remainder is held in trust by the Commissioner of State Lands for the former owner. (26 CAR 400-401; source)
Selling in Arkansas?
We buy Arkansas houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Arkansas sell tax liens or tax deeds?

The statutes and rules describe the sale of the land itself by a state officer, and they bar sales by the county. Under Ark. Code 26-37-101, tax-delinquent land cannot be sold at the county level.

The county collector holds the delinquency for a year. If the owner has not redeemed by the certification date, the collector sends the parcel to the Commissioner of State Lands, who collects the taxes or sells the property at public auction. A buyer at that sale receives a deed from the state, not a certificate that earns interest, so the rest of this page follows the deed path.

What is the timeline from missed payment to state auction?

More than two years can pass between the missed due date and a sale, because the state receives the parcel about a year after the due date and a sale cannot come earlier than one year after that. The steps below come from 26-37-101 and the Commissioner's rules.

StepWhat happens
October 15Taxes become delinquent
One year laterCounty collector holds, then certifies the land after notice
By July 1 of the next yearLatest certification date
On receipt of certificationTitle vests in the State of Arkansas, in care of the Commissioner
At least 30 days before saleCertified mail notice of the sale and the right to redeem
At least 60 days before sale (homestead)Personal service if there is no proof of receiving the mail
At least 1 year after certificationEarliest sale date

Certification names all taxes, penalties, interest and costs, along with the owner of record and last known address. The Commissioner does not take physical possession and has no duty to maintain the property, so upkeep of the house stays with whoever occupies it.

Who must be notified before the sale?

The owner and the interested parties of record must be notified, first by certified mail. Section 26-37-301 sets the notice rules, and the Commissioner's rules add a newspaper publication.

  • If the certified mail comes back unclaimed or refused, the Commissioner resends by regular mail.
  • If it is undelivered for another reason, a second notice goes to any other address in county property records, such as the one on the deed or a forwarding address held by the collector or assessor.
  • For joint tenants every owner counts, and for tenants by the entirety either spouse counts.
  • A homestead owner who cannot be shown to have received the mail is served in person at least 60 days before the sale, and that owner pays the extra cost.

The notice gives a short legal description, the parcel number, the sale date and a warning that the land will be sold unless redeemed. The notice goes to the owner of record at the last known address, so an heir who never updated the records may not see it. Only a person who did not receive notice in substantial compliance can challenge it.

How do you redeem tax-delinquent land?

Pay the taxes, penalties, interest and costs, with a petition, before 4:00 p.m. Central on the last business day before the sale. The Commissioner's real estate division accepts payment online through its Pay Taxes button, or by check or money order with a signed petition to redeem.

  • You need the parcel number from your tax bill.
  • Partial or incorrect payments are rejected and do not extend the deadline.
  • A quoted payoff stays valid for 30 days.
  • Anyone may redeem, and redeeming does not change who owns the property.

The division's phone is 501-324-9422, and its office is at 7003 Valley Ranch Drive in Little Rock. A redemption deed is issued when the payoff is made, and a receipt goes to a redeemer who is not the record owner.

How do the auctions work?

Parcels first go to a public in-person auction, and any that do not sell move to an online auction about 30 days later. The Commissioner's rules, in the 2023 edition on Cornell's site, set out the bidding terms.

  • Bidders register, get a bid card and show photo identification.
  • The highest bid at or above the minimum wins, and an accepted oral bid is binding.
  • Payment is due at the sale by check, certified funds or card. Cash and installment plans are not accepted.
  • Online, the winner pays $100 earnest money, or the whole bid if it is under $100, and the balance in certified funds within 10 business days.
  • State staff, the county collector or deputy, foreign-address entities, and former owners or interested parties cannot bid.

The bar on former owners matters to sellers. Once a house reaches auction, the owner cannot buy it back at the sale. Redemption before the sale is the only route to keep it.

What does the winning bidder actually get?

A limited warranty deed that conveys only the State's interest, and the rules note that it often requires a court action to quiet title. The deed is issued after full payment and recorded with the county.

The Commissioner's rules also describe a 90-day litigation period. That means a buyer at the state's sale receives less than an ordinary seller would convey. For parcels that go unsold at the first auction, the online reserve bid equals the taxes and costs for the first two years, a figure tied to the debt and not to the house's value.

Money bid above taxes, fees, penalties, interest and costs is excess proceeds. The rules pay the Commissioner's costs and the county's taxes first, then other government claims, and send the remainder to the former owner, less up to $500 for administration. Claims are denied unless every requirement is met strictly, and the rules show some inconsistency on the claim period, so check the current rule before counting on a timeline.

What else shows up on the way to certification?

The county collector publishes lists before the state ever sees the parcel. Craighead County's page says the collector prepares a list of delinquent personal property taxes before December 1 each year for a legal newspaper, which must publish it within seven days, and that delinquent real estate taxes are listed in a local newspaper after the deadline.

The Commissioner's division also keeps the county certification books and researches the title of each certified parcel before it notifies owners and interested parties. Each of those is a point where an owner can still catch the problem and pay the county or the state. The sooner a payoff is requested, the fewer months of penalty and interest it carries.

  • Check the newspaper list in your county after October 15.
  • Keep the mailing address on the tax bill current.
  • Look up the parcel number on your latest tax bill before calling any office.

Can you sell the house before it is certified or sold?

Yes, a sale at any point before the auction takes the parcel out of the process once the taxes are paid. Because anyone may redeem, a buyer can pay the redemption amount, and a title company can arrange that payoff from the sale proceeds.

  • Before certification: pay the county collector, and the title company can take the payoff from the sale proceeds.
  • After certification: request a payoff from the Commissioner by parcel number, and note the 30 day quote window.
  • Close before the cutoff, which is 4:00 p.m. Central the last business day before the sale.

Cash Home Buyers makes as-is offers on Arkansas houses with back taxes. Keep your parcel number and the sale date from your notice at hand, because the cutoff time controls what is possible.

More questions about Arkansas Tax Deed and Tax Lien Sales

Can the county sell my house for unpaid taxes in Arkansas?

No. Section 26-37-101 says tax-delinquent land cannot be sold at the county level. The county certifies it to the Commissioner of State Lands, and the state sells it at auction.

When does the state take title?

When the Commissioner receives the county's certification, which must happen by July 1 of the year after the one-year delinquency period. Title vests in the State of Arkansas, in care of the Commissioner.

What is the last moment to redeem?

4:00 p.m. Central on the last business day before the auction. Partial payments are rejected and do not extend the deadline.

Can I bid on my own house at the auction?

No. The Commissioner's rules bar former owners and interested parties from bidding.

Do I get the extra money if the house sells for more than I owe?

Possibly. Excess proceeds go first to the Commissioner's costs, the county's taxes and other government claims, then to the former owner minus up to $500 for administration, but you must file a claim that meets every requirement.

Does redeeming transfer ownership to the person who pays?

No. The Commissioner's division states that redeeming does not change ownership, and anyone may pay on a parcel.
